notes.C01: Two-witness seam detector with a generated tamper bench serves both the fact-check and the crashed-demo jobs; the hum witness may not exist on phone reels.
notes.C02: A fresh sense (which layer a voice lives on) from signals the mono decode erases, but it needs a native-rate/stereo read and many witnesses agreeing.
notes.C03: Inverting forensics into a dub acceptance test, with the original as an exact answer key, is surprising and hits a real owner job.
notes.C04: Per-speaker baselines avoid the rejected emotion labels; useful but mostly a recombination of numbers already computed.
notes.C05: Directly attacks the bench's one shared miss with a cheap word-anchored gate and a premise check before building.
notes.C06: Agent recording its own UI work turns the rarest input into the commonest with a free exact answer key.
notes.C07: First-frame OCR of lasting text closes a plain, cheap gap (claim banners never reach the card); caret crops fit the code-screencast zooms.
notes.C08: Card that survives truncation is a real delivery fix; segment log and trim ladder are more radio-craft than new sense.
notes.C09: Checking the agent's own deliverables against its known intent matches real use, but bundles many loosely related checks.
notes.C10: Repeat and cross-file alignment answers new questions (replays, edit lists), but ENF and compilation phase splitting are speculative.
notes.C11: A Blind ledger that stops a silent card reading as 'authentic', judged by ablation, is a sharp and honest idea.
notes.C12: Sound process for choosing senses, but it adds no new perception itself.
notes.C13: Absence of conversational flaws as evidence of assembly is the most surprising reframe; value limited to a narrow fact-check case.
notes.C14: Concrete, on-demand noun check from a real moment, but open-vocabulary image matching echoes a rejected approach and adds little combination.
notes.C15: Contact sound sync is neat, but stereo pan on a mono pipeline and narrow demand keep its value low.
